paras: The lynching of James Anderson was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a telegraph pole in front of the court house in Pine Bluff, Arkansas, on December 4, 1880. Anderson, accused of raping the wife of a Pine Bluff butcher and robbing her house that morning, was taken by force from the officers who had brought him back under arrest. Southern papers presented the hanging as "speedy justice", and wire summaries carried it to papers from Virginia to Kansas and Wyoming.

According to a Pine Bluff special to the Little Rock Gazette, at six o'clock on the morning of December 4 a Black man entered the back door of the house of Joe Miller, a butcher, who had left the door unlocked. The intruder was said to have choked and raped Mrs. Miller, who was in bed with two children, and to have taken a twenty-dollar and a three-dollar gold piece and some jewelry from a wardrobe. The dispatch reported that the people "felt highly indignant" and that the telegraph was used to spread the alarm.

The accused man boarded the morning train for Arkansas City. The Memphis Appeal reported that Sheriff Bankston of Desha County, who knew him as "an old offender", questioned him on the train at Walnut Lake and arrested him on suspicion. Between Walnut Lake and Arkansas City, Anderson jumped from the train, but a Black brakeman chased him for nearly half a mile and returned him to the guard. At three in the afternoon the Gazette correspondent wrote that the prisoner was on his way back in irons, "strongly guarded", and that there was "no telling what his fate may be."

A postscript timed 7:30 p.m. said that when the train arrived the prisoner was taken to Mrs. Miller's bedside, where she recognized him, and the family identified jewelry and a three-dollar gold piece found on him. He was then "taken by force from the officers" and hanged on a telegraph pole in front of the courthouse. The Appeal's version differed in order: a "committee of ten prominent citizens of Jefferson county" flagged the train outside town, took Anderson from the baggage car, rode the detached locomotive into Pine Bluff, and had him identified before conveying him to Barraque street. Anderson refused to confess, and his only words were "Lord, have mercy!" as he was hauled up.

A notice placed on the body said it was to hang for three days, but it was taken down and buried after about twenty-four hours. The Appeal said a sum of money was collected and given to the brakeman who had prevented the escape. No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The first word in Memphis came from a private letter, which the Public Ledger summarized as the hanging of an unnamed man "in accordance with the lynch law meted out to rapists in Arkansas", adding "A mob did it." The same page carried the Gazette special under the headline "SPEEDY JUSTICE: A Negro Fiend Swung to a Telegraph Pole", and a New Orleans Times version of that dispatch reached Hazlehurst, Mississippi. The Memphis Appeal account, reprinted by the Jackson Weekly Clarion under "Up A Telegraph Pole For the Ravisher", said Anderson "expiated his atrocious crime" and that the execution was "conducted in an orderly manner" with the approval of "the entire population, white and black."

Outside the South the story ran as brief wire items in papers in New Haven, Washington, Richmond, Alexandria, Lancaster, Concord and Westminster, Maryland. These items repeated the accusation as fact, used terms such as "negro fiend" and "desperado", and offered no comment on the lynching. The story kept circulating as filler, reaching the Cheyenne Daily Leader in March 1881 and the Jackson Comet in December 1881.

Accounts disagreed on the date: the Pine Bluff specials and the Appeal placed the assault and the hanging on Saturday, December 4, while a wire dispatch datelined December 5 and the summaries drawn from it said Sunday morning. The dated specials, with their afternoon and 7:30 p.m. entries, are the more direct evidence for December 4. One version of the wire called the husband "James Miller", and two northern summaries printed the town as "Alpine Bluff".

bases: Anderson, under arrest and in the hands of officers, was taken by force and hanged to a telegraph pole in front of the court house (A2, A10, A18).

Anderson was taken by force from the officers holding him and hanged without trial by a mob or a 'committee of ten prominent citizens' (A2, A18), on the accusation of rape and robbery, a hanging one paper called 'the lynch law meted out to rapists in Arkansas' (A1).

Independent dispatches to the Little Rock Gazette and New Orleans Times (A2, A15), a private letter to Memphis (A1), the Dec. 5 wire (A3, A6) and the Memphis Appeal account (A18) agree that Anderson was hanged by a mob to a telegraph pole in front of the Pine Bluff court house.

The Memphis Appeal account, reprinted by the Jackson Weekly Clarion, said Anderson 'expiated his atrocious crime' in an 'orderly' execution approved by the whole population.
Northern papers ran short wire items ('A DESPERADO LYNCHED', 'Hung to a Telegraph-Pole') that treated the accusation as fact without comment.

info: Assault Saturday, Dec. 4, 1880, about 6 a.m.; lynching that evening after the 7:30 p.m. train (Dec. 4 dispatches and Memphis Appeal); a Memphis letter says Saturday morning; the Dec. 5 wire and its summaries say Sunday morning, Dec. 5.
Telegraph pole in front of the court house, on Barraque street, Pine Bluff; the assault was at the Miller house in the eastern suburb.
James (Jim) Anderson, described as 'a negro' and 'colored'.
Accused of entering the house of Joseph (Joe) Miller, a butcher, choking and raping Mrs. Miller, and stealing a $20 and a $3 gold piece and jewelry ($23 in all).
'A mob' (A1, A7); 'the citizens' (A10); a 'committee of ten prominent citizens of Jefferson county' (A18); 'infuriated citizens' (A22). No one is named.
